query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is primarily governed by the accumulation and transmission of dislocations at the nanoscale multilayer interfaces. These interfaces, due to compositional complexity and severe lattice distortion, act as barriers that promote local dislocation pile-up and activate alternative slip mechanisms (such as non-basal slip or deformation twinning) when the local stress concentration exceeds a critical level.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coatings composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers with coherent or semi-coherent interfaces, exhibiting significant compositional complexity and lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Application of sustained mechanical loading (creep test) at controlled stress levels and temperature, with a parallel controlled modification of interface structure (e.g., by tuning processing parameters or introducing minor interface alloying adjustments).
generation.conditions: Room or moderately elevated temperature to avoid thermal activation of extraneous diffusion effects, with sustained load applied over an extended period to enable creep.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale multilayer interfaces that act as dislocation barriers and sites for stress concentration, mediating dislocation interactions and locally activating alternative slip systems.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained stress, dislocations nucleate and move within the individual FCC/BCC layers but are impinged at the interfaces. The resulting pile-ups increase local stresses, eventually triggering secondary deformation mechanisms (such as non-basal slip or twinning) to accommodate plastic flow, thereby gradually changing the effective deformation mode. This process is accentuated by the inherent lattice distortion and short-range ordering present in high-entropy alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous dislocation distribution and conventional slip behavior, the multilayer HEA will show an evolving microstructure with significant evidence of dislocation pile-up at interfaces, a shift to alternative slip/twinning mechanisms, and a measurable increase in creep rate over time. These features would be more pronounced in samples with intentionally less coherent (or more distorted) interfaces.
generation.baseline: The undeformed multilayer state where dislocation motion occurs by conventional slip systems and without significant interface-mediated piling up.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant only under conditions where (1) the applied stress exceeds the level necessary for significant dislocation accumulation at nanoscale interfaces and (2) the interface structure remains essentially nanoscale without complete diffusion or coarsening. Conventional multilayers without the pronounced compositional complexity and lattice distortion may not show the same progression.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between interface structure and the shift in deformation mechanisms remains uncertain, as does the extent to which alternative slip systems (or twinning) become dominant. In addition, the relative contribution of potential phase transformation effects under long-term loading is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Design an experiment comparing two sets of HEA multilayer samples: one set with as-deposited coherent interfaces and another set where interfaces are deliberately modified to be more amorphous or less coherent while retaining nanoscale thickness. Subject both sets to identical sustained load (creep) conditions and monitor the evolution of dislocation structures using in-situ TEM as well as post-mortem microstructural analysis.
measurements: Creep rate and degree of plastic strain over time
Dislocation density and pile-up characteristics at interfaces
Identification of active slip systems (conventional versus non-basal/twinning) via diffraction patterns
Changes in interface structure via high-resolution microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the coherent-interface and modified-interface samples exhibit similar creep rates, dislocation structures, and slip system activations (i.e., no significant difference in the deformation response attributable to interface characteristics), then the hypothesis that interface-mediated dislocation pile-up governs the progressive plastic deformation would be falsified.

Small-Scale Insight into Uniform Deformability and Softening Resistance of Refractory High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Owing to the outstanding softening resistance and thermal stability of BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs), their unique deformation-induced defect structures merit investigation. Therefore, this study evaluated the mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of W-based low- to high-entropy alloys at various temperatures and orientations using nanoindentation and microcompression, complemented by post-mortem TEM and atomistic simulations to observe dislocation populations and their evolution. Results reveal that HEAs exhibit reduced elastic and plastic anisotropy while retaining high-temperature strength. With increasing compositional complexity, planar slip and abrupt stress drops were progressively replaced by homogeneous flow and smoother serrations. Severe lattice distortion promoted dislocation nucleation but impeded long-range glide, enabling cooperative edge and screw dislocation activity that sustained strength and work hardening across temperatures.

Dislocations and deformation microstructure in a B2-ordered Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are multicomponent metallic materials currently attracting high research interest. They display a unique combination of chemical disorder and crystalline long-range order, and due to their attractive properties are promising candidates for technological application. Many high-entropy alloys possess surprisingly high strength, occasionally in combination with high ductility and low density. The mechanisms effecting these attractive mechanical properties are not understood. This study addresses the deformation mechanism of a Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy, which is a two-phase material, consisting of a B2-ordered matrix and disordered body-centred inclusions. We quantitatively analyse the microstructure and dislocations in deformed samples by transmission-electron-microscopic methods including weak-beam imaging and convergent-beam electron diffraction. On the evolving nature of c/a ratio in a hexagonal close-packed epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys

Abstract: Activation of different slip systems in hexagonal close packed (h.c.p.) metals depends primarily on the c/a ratio, which is an intrinsic property that can be altered through alloying addition. In conventional h.c.p. alloys where there is no diffusion-less phase transformation and associated transformation volume change with deformation, the c/a ratio remains constant during deformation. In the present study, c/a ratio and transformation volume change of h.c.p. epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys (HEAs) were quantified as functions of alloy chemistry, friction stir processing and tensile deformation. The study revealed that while intrinsic c/a is dependent on alloying elements, c/a of epsilon in transformative HEAs changes with processing and deformation. This is attributed to transformation volume change induced dependence of h.c.p. lattice parameters on microstructure and stress state. Lower than ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c + a〉 slip and deformation twinning in epsilon phase of transformative HEAs.
